summary: Hams Bluff Light, St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands: a Danish steel lighthouse of 1912-1913, manned until 1974, still a daytime landmark beside a 2011 LED light.

lens.note: VLB-44 LED beacon on the 2011 skeletal tower (NRHP p. 19). The original 1913 fourth-order Fresnel lens was replaced in 1949 (p. 8); the nomination does not say where it went.

structures.note: Danish-built steel lighthouse, 30 ft (9 m) tall, two stories with a lantern; now a daytime landmark (NRHP pp. 4, 9, 19).
Holds the operating LED beacon. The nomination gives its height as 20 ft (p. 4) and 25 ft (p. 19).

Two keepers' dwellings, an oil house (75 ft west of the lighthouse) and a storehouse on the lower ground (NRHP pp. 7, 9, 18). The original buildings were demolished; a modern building now houses VI National Guard functions.

access.note: Accessible on foot (NRHP pp. 4, 12). The route the hiking guide describes crosses National Guard grounds, through a gate that is usually closed; do not pass a closed gate. Whether the tower interior is open to visitors is not stated.

corrections.why: The nomination says the property is owned by the U.S. Coast Guard, which has run the aid since 1939 (pp. 4, 19). The Navy held the lights from 1916 to 1919 and the Navy held 22.25 acres from 1981 (pp. 15, 19).
The nomination says the Hams Bluff Light today continues to serve as a Coast Guard aid to navigation, with a 2011 LED beacon (p. 19).

The nomination says the light station was officially established on 15 July 1913 and began operating in 1913 (pp. 4, 18). The 1915 date comes from the USLHS record, which cites Wikipedia as its source.
Built 1912 to 1913 by the Danish Lighthouse Service (pp. 4, 18).
The nomination says the previously operating optic was removed from the lantern in 2011, when the new tower was erected (p. 19).

corrections.why: The nomination says the skeletal tower and LED beacon were installed in 2011 (p. 19).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The USLHS record gives 'Year Established: 1915', and its listed source is Wikipedia. The nomination says the light was officially established on 15 July 1913 and began operating in 1913. The facts block uses 1913.

The nomination says the U.S. Navy operated the lights from 1916 until after the war, and the Bureau of Lighthouses took ownership in 1919. The Commissioner's report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1918 says the military governor formally transferred care and maintenance to the Lighthouse Service on 16 August 1917. Both are cited; the story presents the disagreement.

The nomination gives August 1974 (pp. 7, 19). The NPS review sheet says the station 'continued as a manned station until 1970'. The facts block uses 1974, the nomination's date; the story states the disagreement.
The nomination gives the 2011 skeletal tower as 20 feet (p. 4) and as 25 feet (p. 19). Neither is used in the facts block's height field; the note keeps both.

The nomination says visible for 14 miles in clear weather, without naming statute or nautical miles. The facts block keeps the record's 14.0 nm. The original 1913 optic is given as 25 nautical miles (p. 18).
The record's 'Fl W 30s' matches the nomination's 'two white flashes every 30 seconds' (p. 19). The facts block writes the standard notation Fl(2) W 30s.

The nomination places the oil house on the lower terrain with the other auxiliary buildings (pp. 7, 18) but also says the oil house was 'located atop Hams Bluff, 75 feet west of the lighthouse' (p. 9). The story states both; the checker did not choose.

notes_for_editor: Keeper names come from the USLHS place roster (NARA Registers of Lighthouse Keepers via the Kraig Anderson inventory). The cached USLHS place page (fetched 2026-10-27) carries no note on confirmation, so the names are as printed and not yet checked against the NARA registers. The story names only a few; the keepers list shows all 23 roster lines as printed, plus A. L. F. Madsen from the nomination. Lines after about 1960 are printed as the archive prints them, with no personal detail added. The Danish-era keepers (1913-1917) other than Madsen are not in the roster and were not found in any source read. The record's 'Fl W 30s' and '14.0 nm' are kept, but the nomination does not name the range unit. Popular travel pages (AllTrails and similar) repeat a 1915 first-lit date; the USLHS record's 1915 cites Wikipedia; the nomination gives 1913 and is used. The 2011 tower height is given as 20 ft (p. 4) and 25 ft (p. 19) in the same nomination. The Commissioner of Lighthouses report for fiscal 1918 lists 'Hams Bluff, St. Croix, Virgin Islands' in a table of aids (scan p. 344, printed p. 30); it is not used in the story. The hiking guide (stcroixhiking.org) describes the walk past the Virgin Islands National Guard facility and a gate 'usually closed'. The story gives no directions and tells readers not to pass a closed gate. The NRHP reviewer's comments (Jim Gabbert, 16 September 2019) and the Legislature's letter are cited as attached to the nomination. The optic maker's name is OCR'd as 'Benard' in the nomination; the story uses the accent. Coordinates: the record's position (OSM) is about 1.4 km from the USLHS point. The nomination gives no coordinates; not checked.
